$comment: Body sections. Build the atoms (service-card, team-card) before the grids that compose them.

service-card.description: Atom. One service. Composed by service-grid — never placed directly in a layout.

icon-top.description: Icon, title, body, link. The default. Cheapest and fastest.

image-top.description: Photo above the title. Use when the service is visually distinctive — reconstruction, procedures, programs.

glass.description: Depth 2. Translucent fill, 1px inner highlight, hover tilt. The single most 'expensive-looking' cheap effect in the library.
notes: Hover: rotateX/rotateY at var(--gf-depth-tilt-deg) with perspective on the grid parent. Sub-degree amounts read premium; large amounts read as a 2013 jQuery plugin.
Requires something behind it — glass over a flat white surface just looks grey.

numbered.description: Large ordinal instead of an icon. Good where services form a sequence or a tiered offering.

a11y: Heading level is h3 — cards live under an h2 section heading.
The whole card may be clickable, but the link text must still be discernible; do not rely on the card as the only affordance.
Icons are aria-hidden; the title carries the meaning.
Tilt and transitions are disabled under prefers-reduced-motion.

service-grid.description: The services section. The most-used body component in the library — every layout has one.

cards-3up.description: Three service-cards per row. The default.

cards-2up-large.description: Two large image-topped cards per row. For premium residential and boutique practices where each service deserves real space.

list-detailed.description: Vertical list with longer copy per service. Medical and commercial buyers read — give them something to read.

programs-4up.description: Four compact cards. Combat programs, medical specialties, or a multi-service restoration routing grid.

alternating-rows.description: Full-width rows alternating image side. Long-form, high-trust. Commercial restoration and capability statements.

responsive.768: All grids become single column. alternating-rows stacks image above copy consistently — do not alternate on mobile, it reads as a bug.

a11y: Section h2 precedes the card h3s. Never skip a level.
Perspective on the parent must not create a scroll container — check for horizontal overflow at every width.

proof-stats.description: Numeric credibility band. Usually a dark full-bleed section, which also gives the page vertical rhythm.

band-4up.description: Four stats across a dark band. The workhorse.

inline-3up.description: Three stats on a light surface, no band. Quieter — used on interior pages.

oversized-2up.description: Two enormous numbers. Maximum impact, minimum content — good when the client only has two numbers worth showing.

responsive.768: grid-4 becomes 2×2. Never a single column — four stacked numbers lose all their impact.

a11y: Value and label are read together — group them so a screen reader does not announce a bare number.
Accent-on-dark must pass AA; the medical and restoration skins both need checking here.
invariants: Every stat comes from business.stats[]. Never invent or round up a number — this is a published claim about the client's business.

process-steps.description: Ordered explanation of what happens next. One of the highest-value sections in all three niches because it directly reduces anxiety: 'what happens after I call' / 'what happens at the first visit' / 'what happens in my first class'.

horizontal-3.description: Three steps side by side with connecting rule. Best for a simple, reassuring sequence.

vertical-timeline.description: Vertical with a connecting spine. For longer sequences — insurance claims, procedure recovery, membership onboarding.

numbered-cards.description: Steps as cards. Use when each step needs an image or more copy than a timeline row can hold.

responsive.768: horizontal-3 becomes vertical-timeline styling rather than three stacked cards — the connecting spine is what communicates sequence.

a11y: Use an ordered list where the order is meaningful.
The step number must not be the only indicator of sequence — the copy carries it too.
Connecting lines are decorative and aria-hidden.

before-after.description: Visual proof. The single most persuasive section on a restoration site, and legally sensitive on a medical one.

depth.description: Always 0. The photographs are the effect; depth would compete with them.

slider.description: Draggable divider over a single pair. Highest engagement.
notes: Handle is keyboard operable via arrow keys with role="slider".
Both images are the same dimensions or the reveal misaligns.

side-by-side.description: Labelled pair, no interaction. Fastest and most accessible. Use where the transformation is obvious.

grid-gallery.description: Multiple pairs in a grid, each opening a lightbox. The centrepiece of resto-03.

responsive.768: side-by-side stacks vertically with labels retained. Slider keeps working — it is touch-friendly by nature.

a11y: Every image has descriptive alt naming the condition, not "before" and "after" alone.
Slider handle is focusable, arrow-key operable, with role="slider" and aria-valuenow.
A non-interactive fallback view is available — never lock the content behind a drag gesture.
invariants: Medical use requires documented patient consent per pair and, in most states, a results-vary disclaimer. validate-client.mjs cannot verify consent — the human must.

testimonial-set.description: Social proof. Four variants tuned to how much weight one quote should carry.

carousel.description: Nestable slider. Use when there are more than six quotes worth showing.
notes: slider-nested, not the legacy slider — its children stay editable and stylable with our tokens.

single-feature.description: One long quote, large type, optional portrait. One specific emotional story beats six generic ones — the right choice for premium residential and concierge medical.

quote-wall.description: Masonry of many short quotes. Reads as volume of goodwill rather than individual stories. Good for gyms and commercial restoration.

responsive.768: Grids and walls become single column. Carousel shows one slide.

a11y: Use <blockquote> with <cite> for attribution.
Star ratings need a text equivalent — an icon row alone is not accessible.
Carousel has visible pause control and is keyboard navigable; it does not autoplay under prefers-reduced-motion.
invariants: Medical testimonials require consentOnFile: true. validate-client.mjs blocks the build otherwise.

team-card.description: Atom. One person. Composed by team-grid.

photo-overlay.description: Name and role over the portrait on hover or gradient. Editorial and confident.

photo-above.description: Portrait, then name, role, credentials. The default — clearest and most scannable.

horizontal.description: Photo beside a longer bio. For directory and provider pages where the bio does the selling.

a11y: Portrait alt is the person's name and role, not "team member".
Credentials are plain text, never image-only.
If the card is a link, the accessible name includes the person's name.
invariants: Credentials, rank, lineage and competition records come from client.json verbatim. In the combat niche these claims are checkable by the audience — inventing one destroys the gym's credibility.

team-grid.description: The people section. Optional in the schema but one of the highest-impact sections on any of these sites — real faces outperform anything copy can do.

cards-4up.description: Four per row. Larger practices and coaching staffs.

list-bio.description: Vertical list of horizontal cards with full bios. Provider and coach index pages.

feature-lead.description: One person featured large, the rest in a smaller grid below. For practices and academies where one individual IS the product — concierge physicians, head professors.

responsive.768: All single column; feature-lead stacks photo above bio.

a11y: Section h2 above card h3s.
Filter controls, where present, are real form controls with labels and announce result counts.

pricing-tiers.description: Pricing. Showing prices converts better than hiding them in all three niches — push back on clients who want them hidden.

three-column.description: Three tiers, middle featured. The conventional shape and it works.
notes: Featured tier gets var(--gf-shadow-rim) and, at depth 2, var(--gf-shadow-glow). Only the featured one — glow on all three is what makes a design look cheap.

two-column-featured.description: Two options, one recommended. Best for memberships and concierge plans where choice paralysis is the enemy.

single-offer.description: One offer, one price, one button. The highest-converting shape when there is genuinely one product.

comparison-table.description: Feature matrix. For the dedicated pricing page, not the homepage.
notes: Wrapped in an overflow-x container so a wide table scrolls itself rather than the page.

responsive.768: Tiers stack with the featured tier first — not in its original middle position.

a11y: Comparison table uses real <table> markup with <th scope>.
Price is readable text, never an image.
Each tier's CTA has a distinct accessible name — three buttons all called "Choose" is a failure.
invariants: Contract terms and commitment length appear in plain text near the price. Burying them in fine print is the pattern this system exists to avoid.

schedule-table.description: Class timetable. One of the most-visited pages on any gym site, and the thing prospects check before they ever call.

weekly-grid.description: Days as columns, times as rows. Scannable at a glance, which is what people want.

by-program.description: Grouped under program headings. Better on a program page than a full week grid.

embed.description: Third-party booking widget where the gym already runs one. Iframe in a reserved-height container so it cannot shift the page.
notes: Reserved min-height is mandatory — third-party embeds are the most common CLS source on these sites.
Embed styling is outside our control; do not promise the client it will match the skin.

responsive.768: weekly-grid scrolls horizontally inside its own container — the page itself must never scroll sideways. Below 480px, switch to by-program.

a11y: Real <table> with <th scope="col"> for days.
Times include am/pm — never a bare 24-hour number in a US context.
The scroll container is keyboard focusable so it can be scrolled without a mouse.
invariants: An out-of-date schedule is worse than none. Flag it in the handover as the client's responsibility to maintain, and make it editable without the builder.

gallery.description: Photography. Where the client has real photos this is one of the strongest sections available; where they do not, omit it rather than filling it with stock.

masonry.description: CSS columns masonry. Handles mixed aspect ratios gracefully, which real client photo dumps always have.

carousel.description: slider-nested. For a curated sequence rather than a dump.

grid-lightbox.description: Uniform grid opening a lightbox. Project portfolios and large-loss galleries.

fullbleed-strip.description: Edge-to-edge horizontally scrolling strip. Kinetic and cheap — combat layouts.

a11y: Every image needs real alt text. A gallery of 20 images with empty alt is a serious violation, and axe will fail the build.
Lightbox traps focus, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the trigger.
The scrolling strip is keyboard scrollable.
invariants: All images lazy-loaded except any that could be the LCP element. A gallery must never be the LCP.

faq.description: Objection handling disguised as help. In all three niches this section directly answers what people actually search for, so it earns both conversions and rankings.

notes: accordion-nested, not the legacy accordion — the nestable version's children are real elements we can style with tokens.

two-column.description: Questions and answers laid out open in two columns. No interaction, everything scannable and indexable.

grouped.description: Accordions grouped under subheadings — by service line, by specialty, by program.

a11y: Accordion triggers are <button> with aria-expanded and aria-controls.
Panels are not hidden from search engines — use height/visibility, and never display:none on indexable content.
First item may be open by default; all closed is also fine. Never all open in the accordion variant.
invariants: Answers must be truthful and traceable to client.json. FAQPage structured data containing an invented claim is a compliance problem, not just an SEO one.

rich-content.description: Long-form prose. The workhorse of service pages, procedure pages and service-area pages — which is where most of the organic traffic actually lands.

single-column.description: One measured column. The default and usually the right answer.

with-sidebar.description: Prose plus a sticky aside carrying a CTA, service links or credentials. Best for service and procedure pages where the reader is deep in research.

two-column.description: Prose flowing across two columns. For capability statements and methodology sections where density signals substance.

responsive.1024: Sidebar drops below the prose and loses its sticky positioning.
responsive.768: two-column becomes one — never two narrow columns on a phone.

a11y: Heading levels inside the prose continue the page hierarchy — the generator must not emit an h1 here.
Line length capped at var(--gf-type-measure). Full-width body text is a readability failure.
Links inside prose are underlined, not colour-only.

logo-strip.description: Client, carrier, affiliation or accreditation logos. Cheap credibility where the logos are genuinely recognisable — and clutter where they are not.

static.description: A wrapping centred row. Preferred — it does not move, so it does not distract.

marquee.description: Continuous horizontal scroll. Use only with eight or more logos — fewer looks like padding.
notes: Duplicate the logo set once in the track so the loop is seamless.
Pauses on hover and does not animate at all under prefers-reduced-motion.

responsive.768: static wraps to a tighter gap; marquee speeds are unchanged.

a11y: Alt text is the organisation name.
Marquee stops under prefers-reduced-motion and on hover/focus.
Never the only place a credential appears — logos are reinforcement, not the claim itself.
invariants: Only use a logo the client has the right to display. Carrier and manufacturer logos frequently have usage restrictions; confirm before publishing.
